evidence: id=673 date=18-02-2026 summary=The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has mandated the Unique Transaction Identifier (UTI) for all OTC derivative transactions, effective from January 1, 2027. This directive applies to transactions in Rupee interest rate derivatives, forward contracts in government securities, foreign currency derivatives, foreign currency interest rate derivatives, and credit derivatives, as per the specified Governing Directions. The UTI, a unique identifier for each transaction, must be generated in accordance with the UTI Technical Guidance issued by the Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures (CPMI) - International Organisation of Securities Commissions (IOSCO) in February 2017. evidence: id=None date=29-04-2026 summary=The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has issued Amendment Directions to modify the existing regulations for Urban Cooperative Banks regarding income recognition, asset classification, and provisioning. These changes, effective from July 1, 2026, are in response to the Urban Cooperative Banks (Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025. Key changes include the deletion of paragraphs 48(4) and 48(5) and the insertion of paragraphs 53A and 53B. Paragraph 53A allows for the retention of borrower accounts classified as Standard upon the implementation of a resolution plan, and for accounts that have slipped into Non-Performing Assets (NPA) between the calamity occurrence and the plan's implementation to be upgraded as Standard. Paragraph 53B ensures that accounts restructured under the 2025 Directions continue to be classified as Standard, even if subsequent restructuring is required. Additionally, Chapter IV - Provisioning Norms B1 introduces additional specific provisioning requirements for banks that implement a resolution plan under the 2025 Directions. Banks must make an additional specific provision of five percent of the outstanding debt for borrowers undergoing a resolution plan (89A), and five percent for each instance of restructuring (89B). These provisions can be written back if the borrower pays at least 20% of the outstanding debt without slipping into NPA post-restructuring and without further restructuring (89C). For non-fund-based facilities or facilities in the nature of cash credit/overdraft, the additional specific provisions can be reversed after one year post-restructuring, provided there was no default during that period (89D). Interest income recognition for borrower accounts under a resolution plan (113A) will be on an accrual basis, while for accounts specified at paragraph 53B, it will be on a cash basis (113B). These amendments aim to provide a more flexible framework for Urban Cooperative Banks to manage stressed assets and ensure financial stability.

Borrowing for trading in TDR and transactions in securities is restricted. Repayment of domestic loans classified as NPAs is prohibited. Individuals can borrow from NRIs or OCI cardholders for use in India, with the loan being non-repatriable. The ECB framework specifies eligible borrowers, including those under restructuring or insolvency resolution, and those with pending legal investigations, provided they disclose such information. The Reserve Bank of India has updated its regulations on External Commercial Borrowing (ECB), allowing eligible borrowers to raise ECB from residents outside India, branches of entities regulated by the Reserve Bank, and financial institutions in the IFSC. ECB can be in FCY or INR and may be changed in currency at the prevailing exchange rate or a rate that does not increase liability. Borrowing can take various forms, including FCCB and FCEB, and is subject to a borrowing limit based on outstanding ECB and net worth. The minimum average maturity period (MAMP) for ECB is three years, with a reduced period for manufacturing sector borrowers. The cost of borrowing aligns with market conditions, and prepayment charges or penal interest are also market-driven. ECB from related parties must adhere to the arm's length principle. evidence: id=None date=29-04-2026 summary=The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has issued Amendment Directions to modify the existing regulations for Rural Cooperative Banks regarding income recognition, asset classification, and provisioning. These changes, effective from July 1, 2026, are in response to the resolution of stressed assets as per the 2025 Directions. Key changes include: - Borrower accounts that are classified as Standard after a resolution plan is implemented will retain their classification. Accounts that slipped into Non-Performing Assets (NPA) between the calamity occurrence and the resolution plan's implementation will be upgraded to Standard upon plan implementation. - Additional specific provisioning is required for borrowers whose resolution plans are implemented under Chapter IV-A of the 2025 Directions. A bank must make an additional specific provision of five percent of the outstanding debt. This provision is over and above the applicable prudential provisions, with a ceiling of 100 percent. - For accounts requiring repeated restructuring under Chapter IV-A, banks must make additional specific provisioning of five percent of the outstanding debt for each restructuring instance. - Additional specific provisions can be written back if the borrower pays at least 20% of the outstanding debt without slipping into NPA post-restructuring and without further restructuring. - For non-fund-based facilities or cash credit/overdraft facilities, the additional specific provisions can be reversed after one year post-restructuring, provided there was no default during that period. These amendments aim to ensure that Rural Cooperative Banks can effectively manage stressed assets and maintain financial stability.

evidence: id=None date=29-04-2026 summary=The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has issued Amendment Directions to modify the existing regulations for Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) regarding income recognition, asset classification, and provisioning. These changes, effective from July 1, 2026, are in response to the resolution of stressed assets as per the 2025 Directions. Key changes include: - Deletion of Paragraph 29. - Insertion of Paragraphs 36A and 36B, which stipulate that accounts classified as Standard post-resolution plan implementation will remain so, and accounts that have slipped into Non-Performing Assets (NPA) between the calamity occurrence and resolution plan implementation will be upgraded to Standard upon plan implementation. - Additional specific provisioning requirements: - A bank must make an additional specific provision of five percent of the outstanding debt for borrowers whose resolution plan has been implemented under Chapter IV-A of the 2025 Directions. - For accounts requiring repeated restructuring under the same chapter, a bank must make additional specific provisioning of five percent of the outstanding debt for each restructuring instance. - The additional specific provisions can be written back if the borrower pays at least 20% of the outstanding debt without slipping into NPA post-restructuring and without further restructuring. - For non-fund-based facilities or facilities in the nature of cash credit/overdraft, the additional specific provisions can be reversed after one year post-restructuring, provided there was no default during that period. These amendments aim to streamline the process for resolving stressed assets and ensure that banks maintain appropriate provisioning levels.

evidence: id=None date=29-04-2026 entity=None nature=None link=https://rbidocs.rbi.org.in/rdocs/notification/PDFs/NT57EBA5AE7606B143BA99B580966304424A.PDF summary=The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has issued Amendment Directions to modify the existing regulations for Urban Cooperative Banks regarding income recognition, asset classification, and provisioning. These changes, effective from July 1, 2026, are in response to the Urban Cooperative Banks (Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025. Key changes include the deletion of paragraphs 48(4) and 48(5) and the insertion of paragraphs 53A and 53B. Paragraph 53A allows for the retention of borrower accounts classified as Standard upon the implementation of a resolution plan, and for accounts that have slipped into Non-Performing Assets (NPA) between the calamity occurrence and the plan's implementation to be upgraded as Standard. Paragraph 53B ensures that accounts restructured under the 2025 Directions continue to be classified as Standard, even if subsequent restructuring is required. Additionally, Chapter IV - Provisioning Norms B1 introduces additional specific provisioning requirements for banks that implement a resolution plan under the 2025 Directions. Banks must make an additional specific provision of five percent of the outstanding debt for borrowers undergoing a resolution plan (89A), and five percent for each instance of restructuring (89B). These provisions can be written back if the borrower pays at least 20% of the outstanding debt without slipping into NPA post-restructuring and without further restructuring (89C). For non-fund-based facilities or facilities in the nature of cash credit/overdraft, the additional specific provisions can be reversed after one year post-restructuring, provided there was no default during that period (89D). Interest income recognition for borrower accounts under a resolution plan (113A) will be on an accrual basis, while for accounts specified at paragraph 53B, it will be on a cash basis (113B). These amendments aim to provide a more flexible framework for Urban Cooperative Banks to manage stressed assets and ensure financial stability.

The amendments include the addition of new sub-paragraphs (7) to (10) in paragraph 10, which detail specific events that may trigger a downgrade in the financial instrument's credit rating or internal credit rating. These events include significant changes in the collateral's value, delays in fee payments, and expected changes in loan documentation that could lead to covenant waivers or amendments. Paragraph 54 is updated to state that asset classification will continue to follow the ageing criteria from the 2026 Directions. Paragraph 63 now specifies that restructured accounts will be provisioned according to the 2026 Directions. Paragraph 67 clarifies that provisioning for interim finance during the insolvency resolution process will adhere to the 2026 Directions. Paragraph 72 is amended to indicate that provisioning will follow the 2026 Directions after the specified period. Paragraph 73 is updated to state that the freezing of provisions will lapse if the resolution plan is rejected by the Adjudicating Authority, and asset classification will continue to follow the 2026 Directions. Paragraph 77(5) is modified to ensure that the conditions for implementing a resolution plan are complied with. The explanation to paragraph 96 is updated to define 'farm credit' in the context of the 2026 Directions. Paragraph 103 is modified to clarify that restructuring loans in natural calamity-affected areas should follow the 2018 Directions, with provisioning guided by the 2026 Directions. Paragraph 119(2) is amended to specify that income recognition for NPAs should follow the 2026 Directions. Paragraph 120 is modified to require additional specific provisions for accounts that have availed DCCO deferment and are classified as standard. Paragraph 124 is deleted. These amendments aim to streamline the resolution process for stressed assets and ensure that banks adhere to the latest regulatory requirements.

evidence: id=None date=30-03-2026 entity=None nature=None link=https://rbidocs.rbi.org.in/rdocs/notification/PDFs/NT25449340B3DEA7740ABBD1A8F299F3FCD48.PDF summary=The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has updated its Amendment Directions for Commercial Banks' Credit Facilities, effective from March 30, 2026. These amendments refine the regulatory framework for credit facilities, introducing new definitions and criteria for eligible securities, capital market intermediaries, and other financial terms. The changes aim to enhance the security and stability of lending practices. Key changes include redefining 'Collateral' to encompass assets securing a credit facility, introducing 'Bridge Finance' for short-term funding, and clarifying 'Capital Market Intermediaries' to exclude certain entities. The amendments also define 'Eligible Securities' to include a broader range of investment options, and introduce new terms like 'Loan to Value' and 'Margin' to better regulate lending practices. The amendments impact how commercial banks assess and provide credit facilities, focusing on enhancing the security and stability of lending practices. They introduce new categories of loan against financial assets, including eligible securities, and bridge finance. Acquisition finance is now extended to Indian non-financial companies for strategic investments, with specific conditions regarding control over target companies and financial entities as subsidiaries. Banks are required to establish a Board-approved policy on acquisition finance. For listed companies, the minimum net worth requirement is raised to ₹500 crore, and they must report net profits after taxes for the last three consecutive financial years. Unlisted companies must meet a net worth of ₹500 crore, net profits after taxes for the last three years, and have an investment grade rating from a credit rating agency. If no rating is available, it must be obtained before disbursement of acquisition finance. Credit assessment for acquisition finance must be conducted on a pro-forma consolidated basis, and total bank financing should not exceed 75% of the acquisition value. The acquiring company must contribute the remaining amount from its own funds. Bridge finance can be utilized by listed companies to meet the minimum own funds requirement, subject to specific conditions. Post-acquisition, the Debt to Equity ratio at the acquiring company's consolidated balance sheet level should not exceed 3:1. Control acquisition can be achieved through equity shares, compulsorily convertible preference shares, and compulsorily convertible debentures, with the acquiring company's debt claims ranking subordinate to the claims of the bank extending acquisition finance. Related party restrictions apply, where the acquiring company and the target company cannot be related parties as defined under the Companies Act, 2013. These restrictions do not apply for financing the acquisition of additional stake as prescribed under proviso to 170N. The amendments also introduce a new Section Q, allowing banks to extend credit facilities against eligible securities, with a policy outlining criteria for collateral selection, limits, concentration limits, LTV/margins, and valuation rules. Loans against a bank's own securities, CDs, and equity-oriented mutual funds are subject to specific conditions and restrictions. Banks must implement robust monitoring mechanisms, adhere to prudential limits, and ensure compliance with share holding regulations.
